question: Does God destroy both the righteous and the wicked?
summary: Job 9:22 says God destroys both the perfect and the wicked. Ecclesiastes 7:15 observes the righteous perishing in their righteousness while the wicked prolong their lives. Ezekiel 21:3 has God promising to cut off both the righteous and the wicked from a land. Against this, Ezekiel 18:8-9, 18:19-20, and 33:18-19 insist that the righteous shall live and the wicked shall die — strict moral retribution. The Hebrew Bible contains both views and they do not reconcile.

reconcile.connective: JFB reads the shared calamity as only outwardly indiscriminate: discipline for the righteous, punishment for the wicked, harmonizing with Ezekiel 18.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, juxtaposes Job 9:22, Ecclesiastes 7:15, and Ezekiel 21:3 against Ezekiel 18 and 33 as flatly incompatible answers.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), pp. 88-89 and p. 178
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact verse cluster in two adjacent entries: "Slays the righteous with the wicked / Spares the righteous" (Job 9:22 and Ezekiel 21:3-4 against Ezekiel 18:9,19 and 33:19, pp. 88-89) and "They surely live / Some of them die" (Ezekiel 18:5,9 against Ecclesiastes 7:15, p. 178). His resolution: the 'destroys/cuts off' texts describe only the shared external, temporal fate of a common calamity, while the 'shall live' texts concern spiritual/eternal destiny, so 'there is no collision between them.'

excerpts.excerpt_text: not contradictory of Eze 18:4, Eze 18:9 and Gen 18:23. Ezekiel here views the mere outward aspect of the indiscriminate universality of the national calamity. But really the same captivity to the “righteous” would prove a blessing as a wholesome discipline, which to the “wicked” would be an unmitigated punishment.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies conflict with Ezek 18:4,9 (the retribution-doctrine texts in this cluster) by distinguishing the outward/temporal calamity both classes share from their inward/ultimate fate (discipline vs. punishment) — the core harmonizing move for the whole cluster.
excerpts.source_note_text: righteous . . . wicked--not contradictory of Eze 18:4, Eze 18:9 and Gen 18:23. Ezekiel here views the mere outward aspect of the indiscriminate universality of the national calamity. But really the same captivity to the "righteous" would prove a blessing as a wholesome discipline, which to the "wicked" would be an unmitigated punishment. The godly were sealed with a mark (Eze 9:4), not for outward exemption from the common calamity, but as marked for the secret interpositions of Providence, overruling even evil to their good. The godly were by comparison so few, that not their salvation but the universality of the judgment is brought into view here.
